entry: Capital and largest city of [[Emilia-Romagna]], northern Italy. The seventh most populous city in Italy, it has 391,473 inhabitants from 150 nationalities. Its [[University of Bologna]], established in AD 1088, is the oldest university in continuous operation. [[UNESCO]] recognized the city's lengthy porticoes as a [[World Heritage Site]] in 2021. Bologna is also an important agricultural, industrial and transport hub, and it hosts one of the largest permanent trade fairs in Europe.

Radical Marxist faction of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party. Led by [[Vladimir Lenin]], it split from the Mensheviks at the Second Party Congress in 1903. Formally established as a party in 1912, the Bolsheviks seized power in the [[October Revolution]] of 1917. They centralized power during the [[Russian Civil War]] and became the sole legal party in Soviet Russia after 1921. Under [[Joseph Stalin]], Bolshevism was linked to rapid industrialization and collectivized agriculture.

Physical constant relating the average thermal energy of gas particles to temperature. Named after Austrian scientist [[Ludwig Boltzmann]], it appears in the [[Ideal gas law|ideal gas law]] and in [[Planck's law]] of black-body radiation. As part of the 2019 revision of the [[International System of Units|SI]], it is defined as exactly 1.380649×10⁻²³ joules per kelvin, which defines the [[Kelvin|kelvin]]. It is used to calculate thermal noise in [[Resistor|resistors]].

Explosive weapon using the exothermic reaction of an [[Explosive|explosive]] material to release energy suddenly and violently. Detonations cause damage through ground- and air-transmitted mechanical stress, the impact of pressure-driven projectiles and pressure effects. Bombs have been used since the 11th century, starting in [[East Asia]], where cast-iron shells packed with [[Gunpowder|gunpowder]] date to 13th-century China. In 1221 a Jurchen army of the [[Jin dynasty (1115–1234)|Jin dynasty]] used explosive bombs against a Chinese Song city. In military usage the term refers to unpowered aerial weapons dropped from aircraft, while shells, depth charges and [[Land mine|land mines]] are classed separately. Homemade [[Improvised explosive device|improvised explosive devices]] (IEDs) have been used by irregular forces in asymmetric conflicts. The word derives from Latin *bombus*, from Greek *bombos*, meaning "booming" and "buzzing".

Military combat aircraft for air-to-ground attack with [[Bomb|bombs]], torpedoes or air-launched cruise missiles. Bombers are classed as strategic or tactical. Strategic bombing by long-range heavy bombers aims to diminish an enemy's capacity to wage war by destroying infrastructure or reducing industrial output. Tactical bombing supports offensive operations, typically near troops on the ground or against enemy shipping. The first air-dropped bomb was released by Italian Second Lieutenant Giulio Gavotti on November 1, 1911, during the Italo-Turkish War. Early in the [[Cold War]], bombers were the only means of carrying [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]] to enemy targets. Guided air-to-air missiles forced bombers to avoid interception, so high-speed, high-altitude flight and [[Stealth technology|stealth]] became central to strategic bombers.

Domesticated [[Moth|moth]] species in the family Bombycidae and the main producer of commercial [[Silk|silk]]. It is known as the domestic silk moth, and its closest wild relative is *Bombyx mandarina*. Its larvae, silkworms, feed exclusively on mulberry leaves, preferring those of white [[Morus (plant)|mulberry]]. Sericulture, the breeding of silk moths for raw silk, has existed for at least 5,000 years in [[China]] and spread to India, [[Korea]], Nepal, [[Japan]] and then the West. Domestic moths are entirely dependent on humans for reproduction and have lost their ability to fly. Conventional sericulture kills the silkworm in the pupal stage, when it has spun a cocoon of raw silk 300 to about 900 m long.

American rock band formed in Sayreville, [[New Jersey]], in 1983. Its third album, *Slippery When Wet* (1986), produced two number-one singles, "You Give Love a Bad Name" and "Livin' on a Prayer". The band has sold more than 130 million records worldwide and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2018. Richie Sambora left in 2013, and the band later released *This House Is Not for Sale* (2016) without him. Its album *2020* was reworked to include songs inspired by the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] and George Floyd protests.

Caribbean island and special municipality of the [[Netherlands]] (pop., 2025: 26,552). Bonaire lies about 80 km off the coast of Venezuela and forms one of the [[ABC islands]] with [[Aruba]] and [[Curaçao]]. Its arid climate and location outside the Main Development Region for [[Tropical cyclone|tropical cyclones]] attract visitors. Its reefs are popular for snorkeling and scuba diving and are protected by the Bonaire National Marine Park. The island became a special municipality in 2010, when the Netherlands Antilles was dissolved.

American [[Western (genre)|Western]] television series broadcast on [[NBC]] from 1959 to 1973. Set in the 1860s, it follows the wealthy Cartwright family, who run the fictional Ponderosa Ranch near Virginia City, [[Nevada]], bordering [[Lake Tahoe]]. The series starred Lorne Greene, Pernell Roberts, Dan Blocker and [[Michael Landon]] over 14 seasons and 431 episodes. It was NBC's longest-running Western and the second-longest-running Western on American network television, behind [[CBS]]'s *Gunsmoke*. In 2002, TV Guide ranked it No. 43 on its list of the 50 Greatest TV Shows of All Time.

Italian Franciscan theologian, philosopher and cardinal. Born Giovanni di Fidanza at Civita di Bagnoregio, in the [[Papal States]], he credited the prayers of [[Francis of Assisi]] with saving him from an untimely death in his youth. He entered the Franciscan Order in 1243 and studied at the University of Paris. He was received as master in 1257, taking his degree alongside his friend [[Thomas Aquinas]]. After defending his order against its critics, he was elected seventh Minister General of the Franciscans and was later made cardinal bishop of Albano. His theology aimed to integrate faith and reason, presenting knowledge as beginning in faith, developed by reason and perfected in mystical union with God. Known as the "Seraphic Doctor", he was canonized in 1482, and Pope Sixtus V declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1588.

[[Debt]] security, a form of [[Loan|loan]] with interest usually paid at fixed intervals and principal repaid at maturity. Bonds are issued by public authorities, credit institutions, companies and supranational institutions to finance long-term investment or, for governments, current expenditure. Bondholders are creditors rather than owners, so they are repaid before [[Stock|stockholders]] in [[Bankruptcy|bankruptcy]] but behind secured creditors. Unlike stocks, bonds usually have a defined maturity, and their market price can differ substantially from face value.

Consensual binding or restraint of a partner, practiced within [[BDSM]] subculture. Partners may be restrained with [[Rope|rope]], cuffs, bondage tape or self-adhering bandage, for erotic, aesthetic or somatosensory stimulation. Bondage does not necessarily involve [[Sadomasochism|sadomasochism]]; it may be an end in itself or part of sex. The restrained partner, called a submissive, surrenders control voluntarily to a dominant partner under mutual understanding and [[Consent|consent]]. The letter B in the acronym BDSM comes from the word bondage.

Partial or complete break in the continuity of a [[Bone|bone]]. Fractures may result from high-force impact or stress, or from minimal trauma when conditions such as [[Osteoporosis|osteoporosis]], osteopenia or bone cancer weaken the bone; the latter are called pathologic fractures. An open fracture breaks through the skin, which raises the risk of [[Infection|infection]]. Bone tissue has no pain receptors, but the surrounding periosteum does. Untreated compartment syndrome may require [[Amputation|amputation]] of the limb. Healing begins with a blood clot replaced by collagen, which is then mineralized by [[Calcium|calcium]] hydroxyapatite [[Crystal|crystals]] into bone. Callus shows on X-ray within six weeks in adults, and healed bone is usually 80% of normal strength by three months, though remodeling may take up to 18 months. [[Tobacco|Tobacco]] smoking hinders bone healing.

Reggae, funk and [[Disco|disco]] music group founded in 1974 in [[West Germany]]. It was created by German record producer Frank Farian, who was its primary songwriter and one of its main vocalists. Its four original members were Liz Mitchell and Marcia Barrett from [[Jamaica]], Maizie Williams from [[Montserrat]] and Bobby Farrell from [[Aruba]]. The group sold over 100 million records, with hits including "Daddy Cool", "Rasputin" and "Rivers of Babylon". It achieved eight number-one singles in Germany and two in the U.K.

Federal city in the German state of [[North Rhine-Westphalia]], on the banks of the [[Rhine]] (pop., 2025: 340,226). It was capital of [[West Germany]] from 1949 until 1990 and seat of government for reunified Germany until 1999, when the government moved to [[Berlin]]. After [[German reunification]], the Berlin-Bonn Act kept a significant federal presence in the city, and about one-third of all ministerial jobs remained there as of 2019. Bonn is the birthplace of Germany's constitution, the Basic Law, and of composer [[Ludwig van Beethoven]]. It hosts 20 [[United Nations]] institutions, the highest number in Germany.

[[Wales|Welsh]] singer known for a distinctive husky voice and emotive power ballads. Her single "It's a Heartache" reached number three on the U.S. Billboard Hot 100. In the 1980s she worked with songwriter and producer Jim Steinman, who wrote her biggest hit, "Total Eclipse of the Heart", the lead single from the U.K. chart-topping album *Faster Than the Speed of Night*. She earned three Grammy Award nominations and was awarded an MBE (Member of the Order of the British Empire) in 2022 for services to music.

American outlaw couple of the [[Great Depression]], known for bank robberies. Bonnie Elizabeth Parker and Clyde Chestnut Barrow roamed the central United States with a gang, committing [[Robbery|robberies]], [[Kidnapping|kidnappings]] and [[Murder|murders]] between 1932 and 1934. They are believed to have murdered at least nine police officers and three civilians. A posse led by retired [[Texas]] Ranger Frank Hamer ambushed them in Louisiana. The film *Bonnie and Clyde* (1967), starring [[Warren Beatty]] and [[Faye Dunaway]], was a critical and commercial success despite being highly fictionalized, and it glamorized the pair.

Irish singer-songwriter and activist, lead vocalist and primary lyricist of [[U2]]. Born in [[Dublin]], he has received 22 [[Grammy Awards]] as a member of U2 and has been inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]]. He campaigns against extreme poverty and HIV/AIDS in Africa and co-founded DATA, EDUN, the ONE Campaign and Product Red. He was named one of [[Time (magazine)|Time]] Persons of the Year in 2005 and was granted an honorary knighthood by [[Elizabeth II]] of the [[United Kingdom]] in 2007. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in the [[United States]] in 2025. He has been criticized for bypassing African businesses in his activism and for tax avoidance.

Smallest species of great [[Ape|ape]], and one of two species in the genus *Pan*. Also called the pygmy chimpanzee, it is distinguished from the [[Chimpanzee|chimpanzee]] by longer limbs, pinker lips, a darker face and longer, parted hair. Predominantly frugivorous, bonobos live in about 500,000 sq km of forest in the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]], south of the [[Congo River]]. The river's formation, around 1.5–2 million years ago, possibly led to the species' isolation from the chimpanzee. Along with the chimpanzee, the bonobo is the closest living relative of [[Human|humans]]. The population is estimated at between 29,500 and 50,000 individuals, and the species is listed as endangered by the IUCN, mainly because of habitat destruction and commercial poaching.

First book of the [[Hebrew Bible]] and the Christian [[Old Testament]]. Its primeval history (chapters 1–11) describes the creation of the world, [[Adam and Eve]] in the garden, and the sparing of the righteous [[Noah]] when humanity corrupted the world with sin. Its ancestral history (chapters 12–50) follows the family of [[Abraham]] into [[Canaan]] and, through Joseph, into Egypt. Tradition credits [[Moses]] as author of the [[Torah]], but scholars date Genesis to several centuries later, possibly to the 5th century BCE. Most mainstream biblical scholars consider it primarily mythological rather than historical.

Illuminated [[Latin]] Gospel book of the [[New Testament]], made c. 800. It was produced in a [[Monastery|monastery]] of the Columban tradition in Ireland or Scotland and contains the four Gospels, largely drawn from the [[Vulgate]]. It is regarded as a masterwork of Western calligraphy and the pinnacle of Insular illumination. Its ten full-page illustrations, figures, animals and Celtic knots surpass other Insular Gospel books in extravagance, and its colors include [[Pigment|pigments]] imported from distant lands. The manuscript has 340 leaves and is named after the Abbey of Kells, its home for centuries. It is displayed in Trinity College Library in [[Dublin]], showing two pages at a time.

Last book of the [[New Testament]] and its only apocalyptic book. Written in Greek, it takes its title from the first word, *apokalypsis*, meaning "revelation" or "unveiling". It is framed as letters to seven churches in Asia, followed by visions of events before the [[Second Coming]] of [[Jesus]], including a seven-headed dragon and a seven-headed beast. Its author names himself John and is conventionally called John of Patmos, after the island in the [[Aegean Sea]]. Modern scholars read it as a first-century warning to early Christians not to assimilate into Roman imperial culture.

British literary award for the best single work of sustained English fiction published in the [[United Kingdom]] or [[Ireland]]. The prize was first presented on April 22, 1969, at Drapers' Hall in the [[City of London]]. Its winner receives £50,000 and usually a significant sales boost. Originally open only to citizens of the [[Commonwealth of Nations]], Ireland and [[South Africa]], it has been open to any English-language novel since 2014. The sister International Booker Prize splits its £50,000 between author and translator.

American educator, author and orator. Born into slavery in [[Virginia]], he was freed during the Civil War and in 1881 became the first leader of Tuskegee Institute in [[Alabama]]. He expanded the college by enlisting students in building its facilities, and his 1895 Atlanta Address brought him national prominence. From 1890 he was the primary leader of the African-American community and of the Black elite. His autobiography *Up from Slavery* (1901) became a major text, and in that year he dined with [[Theodore Roosevelt]] at the [[White House]]. He promoted Black businesses, education and self-help rather than direct challenge to Jim Crow segregation. Critics, including [[W. E. B. Du Bois]], argued that he accommodated [[White supremacy|white supremacy]], while supporters credit his emphasis on economic self-sufficiency. Washington also secretly supported court challenges to segregation.

Branch of mathematics and logic using the truth values true and false as variables. Unlike [[Elementary algebra|elementary algebra]], it uses the logical operators conjunction (∧), disjunction (∨) and negation (¬). [[George Boole]] introduced it in *The Mathematical Analysis of Logic* (1847), and it was perfected in the late 19th century by Jevons, Schröder, Huntington and others. In the 1930s [[Claude Shannon]] applied its rules to switching circuits, analyzing and designing them with [[Logic gate|logic gates]]. The algebra is now fundamental to digital electronics and is provided for in all modern programming languages. It is also used in [[Set theory|set theory]] and statistics, and it describes classical [[Propositional logic|propositional logic]].
